newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: ANALYSIS-LITHUANIAN MARKETS EXPECT SMALL S&P RIPPLE.
newsitem.headline: ANALYSIS-LITHUANIAN MARKETS EXPECT SMALL S&P RIPPLE.

text.p: New, improved sovereign ratings from Standard & Poor's for Lithuania are expected to help hold down already declining interest rates but dealers were cautious on how big the effect would be on debt and equity markets.
Standard and Poor's on Monday announced a BBB- rating for long-term foreign currency, an improvement from the BB+ IBCA assigned in January.
"I think it should decrease yields, for how long is a good question, but probably for the months ahead," said Jonas Irzhikevichius, deputy director of Hermis Bank's treasury department.
"It should be holding in the region of 7.20 percent to 8.85 percent for three-month T-bills and a little bit higher for half-year," Irzhikevichius said.
But observers say there was already a downward trend on yields before Standard and Poor's announced the rating.
Yields on 91-day paper eased Monday to 8.36 percent from 9.21 percent. At Tuesday's auction, yields on 182-day T-bills fell to 8.63 percent from 9.19 percent.
"I don't think this (the declines) were related to Standard and Poor's rating," Irzhikevichius said. "I think it was related to banks which have a surplus in litas."
Reaction to Standard and Poor's rating from share brokers was mixed, with some expecting declining yields to push more money into equities.
"It should make shares more attractive," said Tomas Andrejauskas, a broker with Suprema.
"The T-bills will get more expensive and money will be reallocated to equities," Andrejauskas said.
But another broker cautioned that the new and improved rating came as no big surprise and that it would probably not drive much more money toward the stock exchange.
"I think it was in line with expectations, so probably the market discounted it," said Kestutis Kupshys, a broker with Mendes Prior Europe.

"As turnover and liquidity are lacking on the market, this particular event will not affect it much in the short-to-medium term," Kupshys said. "It makes a very good impression on newcomers, but these newcomers are few."
Lithuania's stock market has languished under low turnover and sliding share prices since the wind was let out of its sails following a January bullrun.
